title: Factor-two approximation for shortest common superstring
formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, given any explicit finite list of strings over an explicitly given finite alphabet, outputs a common superstring of length at most twice the minimum possible length? All occurrences are forward contiguous substrings. The input, zero-optimum convention and full bit-cost model are defined below. The algorithm need not use the maximum-overlap greedy rule.
definitions:
For context, let \(\mathcal R\) be the set of ratios achievable by the deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithms defined below, and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}}=\inf\mathcal R\). 

An instance is an integer \(\sigma\ge1\) and a finite list of finite strings \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) over \(\Sigma=\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}\), where \(k\ge0\). Encode \(\sigma,k\), the length of each string and each symbol in binary with self-delimiting integer fields. For definiteness, encode \(z\ge0\) by a unary prefix giving the bit length of \(z+1\), a zero delimiter, then the binary expansion of \(z+1\). The list contains every symbol explicitly; neither grammar compression nor an oracle representation is allowed. Let \(L\) be the total number of input bits.

A feasible output is an explicit string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) such that, for each \(i\), there are strings \(u_i,v_i\) with \(w=u_i s_i v_i\). Occurrences are ordinary forward contiguous substrings; reversal, reverse complementation, subsequences and cyclic wraparound are not allowed. The objective \(|w|\) counts symbols, not bits. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) as the minimum feasible length. Concatenating the input strings proves feasibility and finiteness. Empty and repeated input strings are allowed. If the list is empty or every member is empty, the optimum is zero, and every finite-factor algorithm must return the empty string. Strings contained in other input strings may be removed by preprocessing, but that work is charged.

An admissible algorithm is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program. For its chosen ratio \(r\), some constants \(K>0\) and integer \(d\ge1\) bound its total steps by \(K(L+1)^d\) on every encoded input. It rejects malformed encodings within that bound. On valid inputs it always outputs a feasible string satisfying the claimed ratio. Reading, preprocessing, integer and symbol operations and writing the complete output all count as bit steps. The program has no advice, randomness or free oracle. Its program and polynomial may depend on \(r\), but not on input size or on the instance.

The infimum is over ratios achievable with one such global guarantee. It need not itself be achievable by a single algorithm. Known constant-factor algorithms make the set nonempty, so \(\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}}\) is finite and at least one. A lower bound on this infimum concerns all deterministic polynomial-time algorithms; a bad input for one particular heuristic is insufficient. No separation assumption such as \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) is built into this existence question. In particular, an algorithmic or hardness claim conditional on an assumption yields only a conditional bound unless that assumption is also proved.

context_blocks.text: Shortest common superstring models assembly by overlaps, with exact containment as the feasibility requirement. Its approximation frontier asks how close polynomial-time assembly can always come to the shortest possible output.

The August 2026 report derives a \(7/3\) general approximation from its cycle-cover inequality and a factor-three greedy guarantee. Tightness of that inequality only limits the specific analysis, not all possible algorithms.

The September preprint claims greedy instances approaching ratio \(9/4\). That refutes a greedy factor-two guarantee if verified, while leaving the existence of a different factor-two algorithm and the full numerical frontier unsettled.

why: A long-standing approximation threshold for a basic string-assembly problem with direct algorithmic genomics and compression motivation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.

progress.text: The ECCC report gives the \(7/3\) general bound and greedy upper bound three; §2.5 states the algorithmic consequence of Theorem 3.1.
Shibata’s preprint claims a greedy lower ratio \((9k+2)/(4k+4)\) for even \(k\ge10\), tending to \(9/4\). This review checks the statement and its scope, not the full counterexample proof.

status_note: The checked primary sources leave the best general approximation ratio unknown. They do not settle the selected factor-two existence question for unrestricted algorithms. The greedy refutation is recorded as a recent preprint claim with its narrower scope. Bounded checks through 18 September 2026 are not an exhaustive certification of current openness.
